chapters.every-day-living.categories.1.i: Diabetes Canada’s guideline describes several styles of eating that work well with diabetes, including Mediterranean, Nordic, DASH and vegetarian
Canada’s food guide suggests plenty of vegetables, fruit, whole grains and protein foods, with protein from plants more often
Make water your drink of choice
Choose whole and less processed foods more often than sugary drinks, fast food and refined grains
Notice when you’re hungry and when you’re full
Culture and food traditions can be part of healthy eating
chapters.every-day-living.categories.1.n: A registered dietitian can help you make a meal plan that fits your culture, your tastes and your blood sugar goals.
Diabetes is the leading cause of kidney disease in Canada. Up to half of people with diabetes will have signs of kidney damage in their lifetime
Good diabetes management and regular screening can prevent or delay the loss of kidney function
Most people have no symptoms early on, so screening is how kidney disease is found
Screening is two tests: a urine test (ACR) that looks for protein, and a blood test (eGFR) that shows how well your kidneys are working
With type 2, screening starts at diagnosis. With type 1, it starts 5 years after diagnosis. After that, it’s once a year
Keeping your blood sugar and blood pressure at target, not smoking, and taking your medicines as prescribed all help protect your kidneys
If you have kidney disease, a dietitian can tell you whether to change how much protein, potassium, phosphate or salt you eat
Ask your team for your ACR and eGFR results, and what they mean for you. Children follow their own schedule, so ask your child’s team.
D · Drugs to protect your heart
Diabetes raises the risk of heart disease and stroke. Heart disease may come 15 years earlier than in people without diabetes
You can lower that risk considerably by working on all your risk factors with your team. Diabetes Canada sums them up as the ABCDEs
A1C is a blood test that shows your average blood sugar over time. Most people aim for 7% or less
Most people aim for a blood pressure below 130/80
The usual LDL (“bad”) cholesterol target is below 2.0 mmol/L
Some medicines protect the heart. Ask your team whether any are right for you
Regular physical activity and healthy eating
Screening for complications in your heart, feet, kidneys and eyes; stopping smoking, with help if you want it; and self-management, including handling stress
Diabetes Canada suggests having your blood pressure checked at every diabetes visit, your A1C every 3 months, and your cholesterol every year, or more often if you take medicine to lower it
Your targets are yours to set with your team. Diabetes Canada notes that A1C targets are different in pregnancy, for older adults and for children 12 and under.
Diabetes Canada’s position is that people with diabetes should be eligible for any job they’re qualified for
It also says people should have the right to look after their diabetes in public places
It says people with diabetes have the right to care that supports the best quality of life wherever they are, including in hospital and long-term care
For a driver’s licence, you have the right to be assessed as an individual. More in Driving
Coverage for medicines, supplies and devices varies across Canada, and you may be eligible for the Disability Tax Credit
Diabetes Canada’s information and support line is 1-800-226-8464
Diabetes Canada publishes position statements on employment, insurance and self-care in public places. They’re linked from its rights pages.
chapters.every-day-living.categories.2.f: Set with (my dietitian or diabetes educator)
chapters.every-day-living.categories.2.i: Diabetes Canada’s guideline suggests learning to count carbohydrate, because how much you eat at one time usually matters
Your body turns carbohydrate into sugar, which raises your blood sugar. Both the kind and the amount matter
Carbohydrate is in grains and starches, fruit, some vegetables, legumes, milk and milk alternatives, sweet foods and many prepared foods. Meat and alternatives, most vegetables and fats have little
Diabetes Canada’s sheet gives about 45 to 60 g of carbohydrate at a meal and 15 to 30 g at a snack for most people. A dietitian or diabetes educator can help you set your own goals
Try to keep each meal and snack within 5 g of your goal
On a Nutrition Facts table, check the serving size first. Then take the total carbohydrate and subtract the fibre: 36 g of carbohydrate with 6 g of fibre counts as 30 g
chapters.every-day-living.categories.2.n: If you take insulin with meals, work out with your team how carbohydrate and insulin fit together. This card covers counting only.
chapters.every-day-living.categories.3.i: Aim for at least 150 minutes a week of activity that raises your breathing and heart rate, like brisk walking, cycling, swimming or dancing
Spread it over at least 3 days, with no more than 2 days in a row off
Start slowly, with 5 to 10 minutes a day, and build up. Less than 150 minutes still has benefits
Add strength exercises at least 2 times a week, with weights, bands or your own body weight. If you’re new to them, get some instruction first
Break up long periods of sitting. Diabetes Canada’s guideline suggests getting up briefly every 20 to 30 minutes
If you’ve been inactive for a while, talk to your doctor before starting anything harder than a brisk walk. If you’re short of breath or have chest pain, stop the activity

Exercise can lower your blood sugar for up to 48 hours. If you take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar, check regularly and carry fast-acting sugar. More in Staying Safe, under Lows that sneak up
chapters.every-day-living.categories.3.n: Ask your team how to plan food and medicines around activity, especially if you use insulin.
chapters.every-day-living.categories.4.i: Diabetes Canada’s alcohol sheet says that, as a general rule, you don’t need to avoid alcohol because you have diabetes. Its newer 2023 guideline adds that if you don’t drink, it’s healthier not to start. Talk with your team about what’s right for you

The sheet says not to drink if you’re pregnant or trying to get pregnant, breastfeeding, have a personal or family history of drinking problems, are about to drive or do anything that needs your full attention, or take certain medicines. Ask your pharmacist about yours

If you take insulin or some other diabetes medicines, a low can come up to 24 hours after drinking. Eat carbohydrate when you drink, check your blood sugar before bed, and make sure someone with you knows how to help, including calling 911 if you pass out. More in Staying Safe, under Lows that sneak up
Alternating alcoholic drinks with water helps you avoid getting dehydrated

Diabetes Canada’s 2018 nutrition guideline gives higher limits than Canada’s 2023 Guidance on Alcohol and Health. Diabetes Canada’s 2023 guideline says that if you drink, cutting down lowers the risk to your health, and the 2023 guidance says that with alcohol, less is better. Your team can help if you want to cut down
Diabetes Canada does not recommend recreational cannabis for teens or adults with diabetes. With type 1, it says to avoid it, because it raises the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
If you do use cannabis, edibles can contain carbohydrate, and cannabis can make you hungrier. Diabetes Canada says adults who use it should be offered advice on lowering the risks
chapters.every-day-living.categories.4.n: Alcohol and cannabis aren’t things to hide from your team. Diabetes Canada asks health-care providers to talk about them regularly, without judgement.
chapters.every-day-living.categories.5.f: If you’re thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, any time of day or night. If your safety is at risk right now, call 911.
If it isn’t easing, or you’re struggling to get through the day
Run by Breakthrough T1D. It lists registered mental health providers.
If you’d like to talk with a mental health provider
chapters.every-day-living.categories.5.i: Living with diabetes can feel like a burden. Diabetes Canada says its constant demands can lead to diabetes distress, low moods and anxiety
You may feel angry, guilty, frightened, discouraged or low. Diabetes Canada’s guideline calls these valid responses to a long-term condition
Depression is more common in people with diabetes, and there are effective treatments
Problems with eating, sleeping and stress are common too. Tell your team about them
So is fear of lows. If it’s holding you back, tell your team, because there are ways to help

Diabetes Canada’s guideline says everyone with diabetes, and parents and caregivers of young people with diabetes, should be checked regularly for diabetes distress. Your team may give you a short questionnaire to fill in before a visit
Regular activity can lower stress and help you relax and sleep
chapters.every-day-living.categories.5.n: If it isn’t easing, or you’re struggling to get through the day, tell your diabetes team or your doctor rather than waiting it out.
chapters.every-day-living.categories.6.i: Keep insulin and your supplies in your carry-on. Diabetes Canada says not to put insulin in checked luggage, because temperature changes can damage it
Insulin, and juice or gel to treat a low, can go through security in amounts over 100 mL. Declare them to the screening officer separately
Syringes are allowed with the needle guard on, as long as you’re carrying the medicine they’re for

Pumps and sensors are allowed. Diabetes Canada says not to wear them through the body scanner or put a pump through the X-ray machine. You can ask for a physical search instead, in private if you like
You don’t have to tell screening staff you have diabetes, and you don’t have to take off your pump. Just tell the screening officer you’re wearing one
CATSA suggests keeping medicine in its labelled packaging. Diabetes Canada suggests a letter from your doctor and a list of your medicines from your pharmacist
Pack spare insulin and supplies. In the heat, keep insulin in an insulated bag. In the cold, keep it close to your body so it doesn’t freeze
chapters.every-day-living.categories.6.n: Crossing time zones can change when you take insulin or diabetes pills. Plan it with your doctor or diabetes educator before you go.
chapters.every-day-living.categories.7.f: If lows are harder to spot
chapters.every-day-living.categories.7.i: These steps are for people who take insulin, or a diabetes pill that can cause lows
Diabetes Canada suggests checking your blood sugar right before you drive, any time you feel low, and at least every 4 hours while driving, or wearing a real-time sensor
Don’t start driving if your blood sugar is below 4.0 mmol/L
After treating a low, wait at least 40 minutes, and until your blood sugar is at least 5.0 mmol/L, before you drive
If a low starts while you’re driving, stop somewhere safe, take the keys out of the ignition and treat it. The 40-minute wait applies here too
Keep fast-acting sugar within reach of the driver’s seat, and your meter and supplies with you

If you no longer feel the early signs of a low, or you’ve had a severe low in the past year, Diabetes Canada’s guideline says to check right before you drive and at least every 2 hours while driving, or wear a real-time sensor

A severe low is one where you pass out or need someone else’s help. If you have one while driving, the guideline says to stop driving right away. Tell your health-care provider and your driver licensing office right away, and do the same if you have more than one severe low while awake in the past 6 months. Your provider may tell you not to drive
You have the right to be assessed for a driver’s licence as an individual. Licensing is handled by each province and territory
chapters.every-day-living.categories.7.n: Diabetes Canada uses 3.9 for a low in most of its guidance, and 4.0 for driving. This card uses 4.0 because the driving guideline does. If your team gave you a number, use theirs.
chapters.every-day-living.categories.8.i: Diabetes can damage the nerves and blood flow in your feet, so you may not feel a blister or cut, and it can be slower to heal
Wash your feet in warm, not hot, water and dry them well, especially between the toes
Check your feet and between your toes for cuts, blisters or changes. Use a hand mirror for the soles, or ask someone to help
Put lotion on your heels and soles, but not between your toes. Trim your nails straight across, not too short
Wear clean socks and well-fitting shoes. Test bath water with your hand before you step in
Have your bare feet checked by your doctor or a foot-care specialist, such as a podiatrist, chiropodist or foot-care nurse. Ask them to check for nerve damage and blood flow too

See your doctor or a foot-care specialist right away for swelling, warmth, redness or pain in your feet or legs, or for corns, calluses, ingrown toenails, warts or slivers. Don’t treat these yourself. An open sore (a foot ulcer) or signs of infection need care promptly, even if they don’t hurt
Don’t go barefoot, even indoors. Don’t use over-the-counter corn or wart treatments, or put hot water bottles or heating pads on your feet
chapters.every-day-living.categories.8.n: If you’ve been told your feet are at high risk, you may need checks more often, and shoes fitted by a professional.
chapters.every-day-living.categories.9.i: Diabetes can damage the small blood vessels in the retina, at the back of the eye. This is called diabetic retinopathy
It often goes unnoticed until it affects your sight, so regular exams matter even when you see well
An optometrist or ophthalmologist does the exam, often after drops that widen your pupils

Diabetes Canada’s guideline: with type 1, from age 15, a yearly exam starting 5 years after diagnosis. With type 2, an exam at diagnosis, then every 1 to 2 years if it finds little or no retinopathy. For a child under 15, ask your child’s team
The Canadian Ophthalmological Society suggests an exam at least once a year, and in the first trimester if you’re pregnant
See an eye doctor right away if you notice dark spots, blurred, distorted or double vision, or large floaters
Found early, retinopathy can often be treated successfully, and treatment can keep your sight from getting worse. Sight that has already been lost can’t be restored, which is why early exams matter
Keeping your blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol in range helps protect your eyes
chapters.every-day-living.categories.9.n: The two Canadian sources on this card suggest different schedules. Your eye-care professional and diabetes team decide yours, and can share your results with each other.
chapters.every-day-living.categoriesIntr: The first half is the everyday: what you eat, how you move, how you feel, and getting around. The second is the checkups that find changes early. If your team gave you different targets or advice, use theirs.
Diabetes, around the rest of your life
chapters.every-day-living.closing.body: Most of this becomes routine: a look at your feet, some movement most days, a few checkups a year. The rest is knowing who to ask.
chapters.every-day-living.focus: Day to day: food, carb counting, being active, alcohol and cannabis, stress and sleep, flying and driving. Protecting your body: your feet, eyes, kidneys and heart, your checkup year, and your rights.
chapters.every-day-living.governance.dis: This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for care from your diabetes team, doctor or pharmacist. Your targets, your medicines and your checkup schedule depend on you. Your team sets them.
chapters.every-day-living.heroBody: Food, movement, mood, travel and driving, then the checkups that look after your feet, eyes, kidneys and heart.
chapters.every-day-living.pharmacist.bod: Liivv’s pharmacist CDEs answer pump and CGM supply questions for all of Canada, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern, except holidays. Your targets, your medicines and your checkups belong with your diabetes team.
chapters.every-day-living.pharmacist.hea: Travelling with a pump or sensor?
chapters.every-day-living.programsBand.c: Type 1, from age 15: an eye exam every year, starting 5 years after diagnosis. Type 2: an exam at diagnosis, then every 1 to 2 years if it finds little or no retinopathy. For a child under 15, ask your child’s team. Your team may set a different schedule: see Your eyes.
A urine test (ACR) and a blood test (eGFR) once a year: from diagnosis with type 2, and from 5 years after diagnosis with type 1. See Your kidneys.

A bare-foot check by your doctor or a foot-care specialist at least once a year, including nerves and blood flow, and more often if you’re at high risk. In between, check them yourself every day: see Your feet, every day.
Blood pressure at every diabetes visit, A1C about every 3 months or as your team advises, and cholesterol once a year. See Your heart: the ABCDEs.
chapters.every-day-living.startHere.head: Today, or the years ahead?
chapters.every-day-living.title: Every Day Living
chapters.every-day-living.urgentExit.lea: Emergencies with lows and highs are in Staying Safe, under
chapters.every-day-living.vibe: Practical and unhurried: how a day works, and what to check each year.
chapters.know-your-type.categories.1.ite: About 10% of people with diabetes have type 1. In type 1, the pancreas makes no insulin, so insulin is taken by injection or with a pump
Type 1 can start in adulthood. Breakthrough T1D says about 71% of Canadians with type 1 were diagnosed as adults
Breakthrough T1D also says 85% have no family connection to type 1
Signs your team looks for include type 1 antibodies in the blood, very little insulin of your own (a low C-peptide), and a risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)

Diabetes Canada’s 2025 type 1 guideline names automated insulin delivery as the preferred option for anyone willing and able to use it. Otherwise, it recommends a sensor (CGM) with a pump or with injections
chapters.know-your-type.categories.1.not: Ketones and DKA are covered in Staying Safe. The test names are explained in Could my type be different?
chapters.know-your-type.categories.10.it: Some single-gene types come with other health signs, such as hearing loss or vision loss
MIDD (maternally inherited diabetes and deafness) passes from a mother to all her children, though how much it affects each child varies. Fathers don’t pass it on
Diabetes starts at 37 on average, and insulin is usually needed within about 2 years
Hearing loss is common and often comes first. The heart, kidneys, eyes and gut can be affected too
A urine sample is preferred for the test
Wolfram syndrome is very rare, about 1 in 500,000 people, and both parents carry the gene. Diabetes usually starts around age 6, and vision loss from the optic nerve around age 11
Lipodystrophy affects where the body stores fat. Clues include little or unusually placed body fat, high triglycerides (a blood fat), and darkened skin in body folds
These are confirmed with genetic testing, arranged through a specialist
chapters.know-your-type.categories.10.no: If several of these sound familiar, ask your team whether a genetics referral would help.
chapters.know-your-type.categories.11.it: Diabetes Canada lists diseases of the pancreas as a cause of diabetes, including pancreatitis, surgery or injury to the pancreas, a growth in the pancreas, and cystic fibrosis
Hemochromatosis, where the body stores too much iron, is on the same list. The Canadian Hemochromatosis Society says it can affect the pancreas and lead to diabetes
About 1 in 300 Canadians have two copies of the gene change that puts them at risk. BC’s guideline says fewer than 1 in 10 of them develop the disease
An iron test isn’t part of a standard blood test, so it has to be asked for. A genetic test confirms hemochromatosis
Close family, such as parents, brothers, sisters and children, should be tested
Treatment removes blood regularly (phlebotomy). The society says it can mildly improve diabetes
chapters.know-your-type.categories.11.no: If you’ve had pancreas disease or surgery, ask your team what it means for your diabetes care. Lows and ketones are covered in Staying Safe.
chapters.know-your-type.categories.12.it: Cystic fibrosis can affect the pancreas and lead to diabetes, called cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD)
It becomes more common with age. In Canada, 3.6% of people with CF under 18 have it, rising to 58.7% of adults over 35

Screening is yearly from age 10, through your CF clinic. Canada’s guideline starts with an A1C test and adds a glucose tolerance test when needed. International guidance prefers starting with the glucose tolerance test. Your clinic decides
Insulin is the main treatment, and the only medicine used for children. Cystic Fibrosis Canada says some adults may have other options

If you use insulin, ask your team for a plan for lows. Cystic Fibrosis Canada recommends glucagon and teaching for people on insulin. International guidance adds that the body’s own response to a low is weaker in CF
In pregnancy, if you don’t already have CFRD, a glucose tolerance test is done early, at 12 to 16 weeks or when the pregnancy is confirmed. If that one is normal, it’s repeated at 24 to 28 weeks
After a transplant, 25 to 50% of people with CF who didn’t have CFRD before develop diabetes
Yearly eye, kidney and nerve checks start 5 years after diagnosis
Your CF clinic works with a diabetes team, ideally including a diabetes educator
chapters.know-your-type.categories.12.no: Glucagon and the Rule of 15 are in Staying Safe.
chapters.know-your-type.categories.13.it: Diabetes Canada lists some medicines that can cause diabetes, including steroids, some antipsychotics and some anti-rejection medicines
Know the signs of high blood sugar and ketones. They’re in Staying Safe
Diabetes Canada’s hospital guideline says 20 to 50% of people without diabetes who take steroids develop high blood sugar. Checking blood sugar for 48 hours after starting may be considered
Some antipsychotic medicines can cause weight gain and raise blood sugar and cholesterol
In children and teens, the risk of type 2 diabetes is 2 to 3 times higher, and the rise can show within the first year
Diabetes Canada recommends checking weight, blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol before you start, then on a schedule that differs for each check. Ask your prescriber when yours are due

International guidance from the American Diabetes Association says to check blood sugar before you start a checkpoint inhibitor, a type of cancer immunotherapy, and at every visit while you’re on it. An international consensus says this diabetes can come on with DKA
After a transplant, the risk depends on things like the steroid dose, some infections, and which anti-rejection medicine is used

Diabetes Canada’s guideline checks blood sugar before the transplant, in the first 3 months after it, and with an A1C at 3 and 12 months, then every year. International guidance prefers a glucose tolerance test. Your team decides
An international consensus says 20 to 40% of people who have a heart, lung or liver transplant develop diabetes
chapters.know-your-type.categories.13.no: Ask your prescriber or pharmacist before you change how you take any of these medicines.
chapters.know-your-type.categories.13.ti: From medicines, or after a transplant
chapters.know-your-type.categories.2.ite: Type 2 is the most common type. Diabetes Canada says 90 to 95% of people with diabetes have it
Risk factors include being over 40, having diabetes in your family, and your ethnic background. Type 2 may cause no symptoms
Diabetes Canada diagnoses diabetes with any one of these results:
A fasting blood sugar of 7.0 mmol/L or higher
An A1C of 6.5% or higher, in adults. It isn’t used when type 1 is suspected
A blood sugar of 11.1 mmol/L or higher, 2 hours after a glucose drink or at any time of day
Without symptoms, a second test on another day confirms it

With symptoms of high blood sugar, Diabetes Canada says the diagnosis is made without a second test, and treatment shouldn’t be delayed. Contact your doctor without waiting. Emergency signs are in Staying Safe
For children and teens with type 2, Diabetes Canada says antibody testing should be considered, because up to 10 to 20% test positive
chapters.know-your-type.categories.2.not: If your diabetes doesn’t fit the usual picture, see Could my type be different?
chapters.know-your-type.categories.3.ite: Prediabetes means a blood sugar above the usual range, but below the numbers for diabetes. Diabetes Canada uses any one of these results:
A fasting blood sugar of 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L
A blood sugar of 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L, 2 hours after a glucose drink
Diabetes Canada’s Prediabetes page links to the CANRISK test
Not everyone with prediabetes goes on to develop type 2, but Diabetes Canada says many people do
chapters.know-your-type.categories.3.not: Ask your doctor what your numbers mean for you, and when to test again.
chapters.know-your-type.categories.4.fig: My glucose tolerance test, between 6 weeks and 6 months after the birth, is booked for
Who orders it, and where I go
chapters.know-your-type.categories.4.ite: Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar first found during pregnancy. Diabetes from before pregnancy, type 1 or type 2, was diagnosed before you conceived
Diabetes that is clearly there early in pregnancy is counted on its own, as overt diabetes, not as gestational diabetes
If you’re at high risk, Diabetes Canada’s guideline includes an A1C test before 20 weeks
Screening for gestational diabetes is offered between 24 and 28 weeks
Diabetes Canada says gestational diabetes affects 3 to 20% of pregnancies and usually goes away after birth. It raises the chance of type 2 and heart disease later
After the birth, Diabetes Canada recommends a glucose tolerance test between 6 weeks and 6 months

International guidance from the University of Exeter says a steady fasting blood sugar of 5.5 to 8 mmol/L, with diabetes in the family, can point to a single-gene type called GCK-MODY. If that sounds like you, tell your team early in pregnancy
chapters.know-your-type.categories.4.not: Fill in the reminder with your team before the birth. Pregnancy with type 1 or type 2 is covered in This Might Be You.
chapters.know-your-type.categories.4.tit: Gestational, or diabetes from before pregnancy?
chapters.know-your-type.categories.5.ite: Type 1 starts before there are symptoms. Breakthrough T1D describes stages 1 and 2 coming before diagnosis, and international guidance defines the stages like this:

In May 2025, Health Canada approved teplizumab (Tzield) for people aged 8 and older in stage 2. Diabetes Canada says it isn’t on any provincial or territorial drug plan. It’s available out of pocket, through private insurance, or through compassionate access
Stage 1: two or more type 1 antibodies, with normal blood sugar
Stage 2: antibodies, with blood sugar starting to rise above normal
Breakthrough T1D says two or more antibodies that last over time mean a high risk of type 1. Only 10 to 15% of people newly diagnosed have a family history

TrialNet screens relatives of people with type 1 at no cost, with a home finger-stick kit or a lab visit, anywhere in Canada. Immediate relatives aged 2 to 45 and other relatives aged 2 to 20 can take part. Results take 4 to 6 weeks
Breakthrough T1D also lists FEDERATE-Can, in Quebec. CanScreen, a Canadian research program on screening newborns and children, says it is launching in fall 2026 or winter 2027
Diabetes Canada’s 2025 type 1 guideline makes no recommendation about screening
People who test positive are followed over time. International guidance says they should be taught, and reminded, about the signs of diabetes and DKA
chapters.know-your-type.categories.5.not: Whether to screen, and what a result means, is a conversation with your doctor. A screening result isn’t a diagnosis.
chapters.know-your-type.categories.6.fig: Test names, in plain words
Where Canadian guidance doesn’t explain a test, the meaning here comes from international guidance.
Tick any that fit you
Questions to bring to your team
Does my type still fit, given the clues I’ve ticked?
Have I had antibody tests? What did they show?
Would a C-peptide test help, and when?
Should anyone in my family be tested?
Would a specialist or a genetics clinic help?
The antibody test most often done first when type 1 or LADA is possible.
GAD (GADA)
Other type 1 antibodies, also used in screening. IA-2 and ZnT8 may be tested if the GAD test is negative.
IA-2, ZnT8 and IAA
Shows how much insulin your body still makes. It’s a blood or urine test.
C-peptide

A blood test that reflects your average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months. Diabetes Canada uses it to diagnose diabetes and prediabetes. With diabetes, it’s usually checked about every 3 months.
A1C
Your blood sugar is checked 2 hours after a 75 g glucose drink.
OGTT (glucose tolerance test)
A genetic test that looks at many diabetes genes at once.
Gene panel
chapters.know-your-type.categories.6.not: Not a diagnostic tool. These clues are things to mention, not signs that your type is wrong. Your team decides what to test. Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change is made with your specialist.
chapters.know-your-type.categories.6.sec: Why the type matters
Your diabetes team decides your type. Diabetes Canada says some cases are difficult to classify

An international consensus from the American Diabetes Association and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes found that more than 40% of people who develop type 1 after age 30 are first treated as type 2
Diabetes Canada says the right type may change your treatment. International guidance adds that it can show whether your family might be offered testing
Clues to mention to your team
You were diagnosed at a younger age, or you’re not overweight
You lost weight without trying, or you’ve had ketones or DKA
You needed insulin within 1 to 2 years of diagnosis
Diabetes runs through generations of your family, such as a parent and a grandparent
You were diagnosed before 6 months of age
You have hearing loss, and there’s diabetes on your mother’s side of the family. International guidance links the two
You’ve had pancreas disease or surgery, or you have cystic fibrosis or iron overload (hemochromatosis)
Your diabetes started after a transplant, or after you began steroids, an antipsychotic, an anti-rejection medicine or cancer immunotherapy
You have a hormone condition, such as Cushing’s syndrome or acromegaly
Tests that can help
Antibody tests look for signs of type 1. International guidance suggests testing for GAD antibodies first
A C-peptide test shows how much insulin your body still makes. It’s most useful months to years after diagnosis, and not during a very high blood sugar
Genetic tests look for single-gene types, such as MODY. A specialist usually arranges them

Diabetes Canada says antibody levels fade over time, and the tests aren’t accurate enough to use for everyone. International guidance recommends them for adults whose features overlap with type 1. Your team decides
Getting tested in Canada
Your doctor or specialist orders these tests. In Manitoba, for example, the GAD antibody test is ordered by endocrinologists, and other doctors need an approval form
What’s covered varies by province. In BC, for example, the antibody tests aren’t covered by MSP
Genetic testing usually needs a referral. A test that isn’t offered in your province may need approval before it’s sent elsewhere
chapters.know-your-type.categories.7.fig: Have I had an antibody test? What did it show?
When should I check for ketones, and how?
LADA: questions to bring to your team
chapters.know-your-type.categories.7.ite: LADA (latent autoimmune diabetes in adults) is a slow-starting form of type 1. It’s sometimes called type 1.5
The usual pattern: it starts after age 30, antibodies are present, and insulin isn’t needed for at least the first 6 months
It’s often first diagnosed and managed as type 2
An antibody test, usually GAD, confirms it. International guidance says a C-peptide test helps guide treatment
Most people need insulin sooner than with type 2, and the timing varies widely. International guidance says it tends to come sooner with higher antibody levels, or more than one antibody
Breakthrough T1D describes a modified type 1 plan, which can include some type 2 medicines. International guidance says others are less suitable, so ask your team before any change
Estimates of how common it is range from 2 to 12% of adult diabetes (an international consensus) to about 10% (Breakthrough T1D)
chapters.know-your-type.categories.7.not: Bring these questions to your team. The signs of lows and ketones are in Staying Safe.
chapters.know-your-type.categories.7.tit: LADA: type 1 that starts slowly in adults
chapters.know-your-type.categories.8.fig: For your appointment. Fill in what you know and leave the rest blank. It doesn’t work out a risk, and nothing you type is saved or sent.
chapters.know-your-type.categories.8.ite: MODY is caused by a change in a single gene. Diabetes UK and the University of Exeter say it’s 1 to 2% of diabetes. The US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) says 1 to 5% of diabetes is single-gene, counting all types
In pregnancy with GCK, care depends on whether the baby inherited it, so tell your team early. HNF4A can mean a larger baby, and low blood sugar in the newborn
In a Canadian study of children with single-gene diabetes, GCK was the most common type: 19 of 29 children
Most of the evidence comes from people of European ancestry. The usual clues are less reliable for people of other ancestries
Diabetes UK says about 9 in 10 people with MODY are first told they have another type
Clues include being diagnosed young, not being overweight, having no type 1 antibodies, and a parent with diabetes, in two or more generations
How young varies. Diabetes Canada and Diabetes UK use under 25. Other international guidance uses under 30, or 35 and under. Your team decides
It’s confirmed with a genetic test, usually after antibody and C-peptide tests
GCK: a mild, steady high blood sugar that usually needs no treatment
HNF1A and HNF4A: often treated with tablets rather than insulin. A specialist decides
HNF1B: can affect the kidneys, with cysts, and other organs. It’s usually treated with insulin
Each child of a parent with MODY has a 50% chance of inheriting it. Once the family’s gene change is known, relatives can be tested, and genetic counselling can help
chapters.know-your-type.categories.8.not: Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change is made with your specialist. Fill in the family tree before your appointment. It helps your team, or a genetic counsellor, see the pattern.
chapters.know-your-type.categories.9.ite: Diabetes diagnosed before 6 months of age is usually caused by a single gene
Diabetes Canada says every baby diagnosed before 6 months should have genetic testing
The University of Exeter says it affects about 1 in 100,000 births. The US NIDDK says about 1 in 90,000, and describes it in the first 6 to 12 months
Some forms are temporary, and others are lifelong

The genetic result matters. For the potassium-channel types, international guidance says about 9 in 10 people can switch from insulin to tablets under specialist care, with more benefit the earlier it happens
Adults told they have type 1 who were diagnosed before 6 months should have their diagnosis reviewed
chapters.know-your-type.categories.9.not: Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change in treatment is planned with a specialist team.
Most people have one of the common types. Some have a less common type, and for some the type becomes clearer over time. This chapter explains each one, and the clues worth raising with your team. Your team decides your type.
chapters.know-your-type.closing.body: Your type shapes your care, and it can be looked at again if something doesn’t fit. Bring your clues and your questions to your team.
chapters.know-your-type.closing.heading: Knowing your type
chapters.know-your-type.focus: The common types: type 1 at any age, type 2, prediabetes, gestational diabetes, and how type 1 starts before symptoms. Less common types: when your type might be different, LADA, MODY, diabetes in babies, genetic syndromes, pancreas conditions and iron overload, cystic fibrosis-related diabetes, and diabetes from medicines or after a transplant.
chapters.know-your-type.governance.discl: This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a diagnosis. Your diabetes team decides your type, which tests you need, and your treatment.
chapters.know-your-type.heroBody: The common types of diabetes, the less common ones, and the clues that your type might be different. Your team decides your type. This chapter helps you ask.

Free type 1 antibody screening for relatives, at home or at a lab, anywhere in Canada. See Type 1 starts before symptoms.

Diabetes Canada says depression is more common in people with diabetes, so looking after your mood is part of looking after your diabetes
Diabetes Canada’s guideline says diabetes teams should ask everyone, from time to time, about diabetes distress and about mood and anxiety. You can bring it up first
Your team will start with what you need to know first. The rest can wait

Your diabetes educator: your plan, your readings and everyday questions. Many are Certified Diabetes Educators (CDE®), licensed health professionals certified in diabetes education
Your doctor: your diagnosis, your prescriptions and your checkups

Who to ask
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.2: Type 1: the pancreas doesn’t make insulin. Diabetes Canada says 5 to 10% of people with diabetes have type 1, and it can start in adulthood too
Type 2: the most common type, 90 to 95% of people with diabetes. It may have no symptoms
Gestational diabetes: shows up during pregnancy, in 3 to 20% of pregnancies. It usually goes away after the birth, but it raises the chance of type 2 later, for you and your child
Prediabetes: blood sugar that’s higher than normal, but not yet high enough to be called type 2 diabetes

Less common types: Diabetes Canada’s guideline lists less common forms, such as LADA (which it counts as type 1) and monogenic diabetes, and says some cases are hard to classify. If your type doesn’t seem to fit, ask your team
Know Your Type has a card for each one, including the less common types.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.3: Time in range, if I use a sensor
Diabetes Canada’s usual targets, in mmol/L
What to do about a low: The Rule of 15
Your team may set different numbers, for example for a child. Use theirs.
Diabetes Canada’s usual targets are 4.0 to 7.0 mmol/L before meals and 5.0 to 10.0 two hours after eating
If your A1C isn’t at target, your team may set a lower after-meal target. Diabetes Canada gives 5.0 to 8.0
A1C is a blood test that shows your average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months. It’s usually done about every 3 months, and Diabetes Canada’s usual target is 7.0% or less
If you use a sensor, Diabetes Canada’s guideline uses international targets: for most adults, more than 70% of the day between 3.9 and 10.0
Your team may set different targets, for example for children, or if you’re pregnant, frail, or often have severe lows
Write your own targets on the card and keep it with your meter. If your team gave you different numbers, use theirs.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.4: Canada’s food guide suggests plenty of vegetables and fruit, whole grains and protein foods, with plant protein more often
It suggests water as your drink of choice, and limiting highly processed foods
Diabetes Canada’s guideline supports more than one way of eating, including Mediterranean, DASH and vegetarian. A dietitian can help you find what fits
Start slowly, with 5 to 10 minutes of activity a day, and build up
Diabetes Canada suggests working up to 150 minutes a week of moderate to vigorous activity, such as 30 minutes on 5 days
If you haven’t been active for a while, talk to your doctor before you start anything harder than a brisk walk
If you take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar, carry fast-acting sugar when you’re active
Carb counting, eating out and more on moving your body are in Every Day Living. If you take insulin, ask your team how to plan around activity.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.5: If they’re at risk of a severe low
Ask what help they’d like. Some people want company at appointments, and some would rather manage on their own
Learn what a low looks like for them, and where they keep fast-acting sugar. The steps are in The Rule of 15, in Staying Safe

If they’re at risk of a severe low, such as people who take insulin, Diabetes Canada’s guideline says the people around them should be taught how to give glucagon, and to call 911. The signs that need emergency care are in Staying Safe
If they have type 1, immediate family aged 2 to 45, and other relatives aged 2 to 20, can ask about free research screening through TrialNet, anywhere in Canada
Your own feelings count too. If you’re caring for a child or teen with type 1, Breakthrough T1D has a Caregiver Guide
More for families and caregivers is in This Might Be You.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.6: Whether you check your blood sugar at home, and how often, depends on your type and your treatment. Your team will tell you what you need
If you take insulin more than once a day, Diabetes Canada’s guideline says to check at least 3 times a day
For type 1 on injections or a pump, Diabetes Canada’s guidelines recommend a sensor that reads all the time (a continuous glucose monitor). Ask your team whether that fits you
A sensor can run up to 15 minutes behind your blood sugar, so Diabetes Canada suggests keeping a meter and strips as a backup
Choosing a meter, and the strips and lancets that go with it, is in Your Tools
Some provinces cover strips and sensors, and how much often depends on your treatment. Funding & Coverage has the details for your province.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.7: What is each of my medicines for, and when do I take it?
Can any of them cause a low? If so, what should I keep with me?
Do any of them need to be paused on a sick day? Diabetes Canada’s sick-day sheet has a space for your pharmacist to write this down
How do I store each one, and how long does it keep once it’s open?
Which supplies go with my medicines, and are they covered by my plan?
Take this list to your pharmacist or your next appointment, with your medicines or a list of them. Your prescriber chooses your medicines. Your pharmacist helps you use them safely.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.8: Diabetes Canada says everyone with type 1, and many people with type 2, need insulin to stay healthy
There’s no one-size-fits-all plan. Your team works out with you how many injections, when, how much, and whether a pump suits you
Insulin can be taken with a pen, a syringe or a pump. Pens come with an instruction book, so read it to learn how yours works
Change where you inject each time. Diabetes Canada says this helps prevent fatty lumps that can make insulin work poorly
Use a new pen tip or needle every time, then put it in a sharps container
Insulin raises your risk of a low. Diabetes Canada says to always have fast-acting sugar with you, at home and when you go out. The steps are in The Rule of 15, in Staying Safe
Storage is different for each insulin. Follow the leaflet that came with yours, or ask your pharmacist
Diabetes Canada says to throw out insulin that has been frozen, has been in temperatures over 30°C, or has expired
Your prescriber chooses your insulin, and fine-tuning your routine takes time. A step-by-step injection guide is in Your Tools.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categories.9: Used lancets, pen tips and needles go in a sharps container. Diabetes Canada says pen tips and needles are for one use only
Sharps include lancets, pen needles, sensor applicators that have a needle, infusion sets and syringes
Never put used sharps in the garbage or recycling, says the Health Products Stewardship Association
In Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, participating pharmacies give out free sharps containers and take them back
Elsewhere in Canada, ask your pharmacy. Diabetes Canada says many pharmacies supply containers and swap a full one for a new one
Ask your pharmacy where to return a full container near you.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.categoriesIn: This chapter covers the first days after a diagnosis, then getting set up. If you’ve just been told, start at the top. If you already have a plan and supplies, start at Do I need a meter?
You don’t have to learn it all at once
chapters.new-to-the-journey.closing.body: New to the Journey is permission to learn slowly: a few numbers, a few supplies, and people to ask.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.closing.head: One step, then the next
chapters.new-to-the-journey.focus: The first days: how you’re feeling, which diabetes this is, your target ranges, first steps with food and movement, and supporting someone. Setting up: meters and sensors, your medicines, starting insulin, sharps, a starter list, and who to ask.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.governance.d: This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for care from your diabetes team, doctor or pharmacist. Your type, your targets and your medicines depend on you. Your team sets them.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.heroBody: Just been told, or getting set up: calm first steps, the numbers your team will talk about, and who to ask.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.pharmacist.b: Liivv’s pharmacist CDEs answer pump, sensor and supply questions for all of Canada, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern, except holidays, and pass you to the right Liivv pharmacy when needed. Your plan and your medicines still belong with your diabetes team.
chapters.new-to-the-journey.programsBand: The first months are for learning, at your own pace. Your diabetes educator can go over your plan, your readings and your questions. With gestational diabetes or prediabetes, your checkups are different, so ask your team which of these apply.
Find a CDE — Canadian Diabetes Educator Certification Board
Diabetes Canada’s guideline suggests an A1C test about every 3 months. For adults whose numbers have been steady at target, your team may space it out. Your usual target is in Your target ranges.

With type 2, Diabetes Canada’s guideline says to have an eye exam at diagnosis. With type 1, for people 15 and over, yearly eye exams start 5 years after diagnosis. Children have their own schedule. Your team tells you when yours is due.

Diabetes Canada’s guideline says two tests, called ACR and eGFR, check your kidneys at least once a year. With type 2 they start at diagnosis. With type 1 they usually start 5 years after diagnosis. Children have their own schedule, so ask your team.
Diabetes Canada suggests washing, drying and checking your feet every day, with a mirror if you need one. At least once a year, your team checks your bare feet, including feeling and blood flow.

chapters.staying-safe.categories.1.items: Diabetes Canada calls a blood sugar below 3.9 mmol/L low
Level 3: a low at any number where you need someone else’s help to treat it
If you use a sensor, Canadian targets for most people aim for less than 4% of the day below 3.9
chapters.staying-safe.categories.1.note: Some Canadian guidance for driving and for school uses 4.0 instead of 3.9. If your team gave you a number, use theirs.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.1.title: Know your low
chapters.staying-safe.categories.10.item: Diabetes Canada suggests an emergency kit with at least one to two weeks of supplies
Include fast-acting sugar, glucagon if you have it, ketone strips and a sharps container
If you use a pump, add a written copy of your settings
Diabète Québec says to keep unopened insulin in the fridge, at 2 to 8 °C. Throw out insulin that has frozen, been above 30 °C, or expired
How long an opened pen or vial lasts depends on the product. Follow the leaflet that came with your insulin
chapters.staying-safe.categories.11.figu: Questions about pump and sensor supplies.
A Liivv service · all of Canada · Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern, except holidays
{count} places fit what you ticked. Everyone stays listed.
{count} place fits what you ticked. Everyone stays listed.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.11.item: 911: someone can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure
Emergency department, or 911: blood ketones over 3.0, large urine ketones, vomiting with no fluids kept down, or signs of DKA such as deep breathing or fruity-smelling breath
Your diabetes team, now: blood ketones 1.5 to 3.0, or moderate urine ketones
Your diabetes team: blood ketones 0.6 to 1.5 when you’re sick, or small urine ketones
Your pharmacist: your sick-day medicine plan, and how your glucagon works
chapters.staying-safe.categories.2.figur: On an automated (closed-loop) insulin system? Diabetes Canada’s type 1 guideline says people of any age may treat a low they can manage themselves with less, 5 to 10 g. Ask your team what to use.
Give fast-acting sugar. The amount for the child’s age is in the table
If it’s still below 3.9, give the amount in the table again

From Diabetes Canada’s guideline for children with type 1 diabetes who use injections, or a pump that doesn’t adjust insulin on its own. Children on an automated (closed-loop) system may need less. Ask your child’s team.
Each of these is 15 g of fast-acting sugar. For a child, give the amount in the table for their age:
Give the amount for their age
Still below 3.9? Give that amount again
Glucose tablets that add up to 15 g
½ cup (125 mL) of juice or regular pop
1 tablespoon of sugar dissolved in water
15 g of fast-acting sugar is one of these:
chapters.staying-safe.categories.2.items: Wait 15 minutes, then check your blood sugar again
If it’s still below 3.9, take another 15 g
Once it’s back up, if your next meal is more than an hour away, have a snack with a starch and a protein
chapters.staying-safe.categories.2.note: After a low, wait at least 40 minutes, and until your blood sugar is at least 5.0, before you drive. More on driving in Every Day Living.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.2.title: The Rule of 15
chapters.staying-safe.categories.3.items: Glucagon is for a low when the person can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure. Someone else gives it
It comes as a nasal spray or an injection. Your pharmacist can tell you which is available
Call 911, or have someone call. Give glucagon, turn the person on their side and stay with them. Don’t put food or drink in their mouth
If a low is affecting the person’s thinking or movement but they can still swallow, Diabetes Canada’s sheet says to give 20 g of fast-acting sugar
At school, staff named in the student’s care plan, and trained, give glucagon when the plan includes consent for it
chapters.staying-safe.categories.3.note: Ask your pharmacist to show you how your glucagon works, and check its expiry date from time to time. For a child under 4, ask your child’s team which glucagon to keep.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.3.title: Glucagon: help someone else gives
chapters.staying-safe.categories.4.items: Exercise can keep lowering your blood sugar for up to 48 hours afterwards
Check your blood sugar regularly, especially if you take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar
If you take insulin or some diabetes pills, alcohol can cause a low up to 24 hours after you drink
Diabetes Canada suggests eating carbohydrate when you drink, and checking your blood sugar before bed
Diabetes Canada says glucagon won’t work while alcohol is in your body. Make sure someone with you knows to call 911 if you pass out
A sensor can run up to 15 minutes behind your blood sugar. Diabetes Canada suggests keeping a meter as a backup
chapters.staying-safe.categories.4.note: Ask your team how to plan your medicines around exercise and drinking.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.4.title: Lows that sneak up
chapters.staying-safe.categories.5.items: Carry fast-acting sugar when you’re active
If you have glucagon, show the people you spend time with how it works. Diabetes Canada’s guideline says they should be taught
Wear medical ID, such as a bracelet or necklace
For a child at school, a care plan made before the school year covers daily care and emergencies, with at least two trained staff
Diabetes@School says to treat a student’s low right away, where it happens, and not to leave them alone
Students may carry a phone or smartwatch to help manage their blood sugar
chapters.staying-safe.categories.5.title: Carry it, wear it
chapters.staying-safe.categories.6.items: Diabetes Canada’s usual targets are 4.0 to 7.0 mmol/L before meals and 5.0 to 10.0 two hours after meals. Your team may set different ones
Symptoms of a high can show up when your fasting blood sugar is 11 or higher
If your blood sugar stays above 14 before meals for more than a few meals, check for ketones
Ketones can build up even when blood sugar is close to normal, for example in pregnancy or with some diabetes medicines. Ask your pharmacist whether this applies to you
chapters.staying-safe.categories.6.note: Very high blood sugar or high ketones need care right away. The signs are at the top of this page.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.6.title: Highs
chapters.staying-safe.categories.7.figur: Keep checking. If you’re sick, call your diabetes team
Risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Call your team now
Risk of DKA. Call your team now
Written for type 1 diabetes, by Breakthrough T1D
chapters.staying-safe.categories.7.items: Ketones build up when your body doesn’t have enough insulin and starts breaking down fat for energy
You can check ketones in your blood or in your urine. Your team will tell you which to use

Check when your blood sugar stays high. With type 1, check when you’re sick too, especially with vomiting, stomach pain or a fever. With other types, check when you’re sick if your team has told you to
Diabetes Canada’s guideline for type 1 diabetes says to put off hard exercise if blood ketones are 1.5 or higher

Signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) include thirst, passing a lot of urine, stomach pain, feeling or being sick, deeper breathing, fruity-smelling breath, and feeling tired, sleepy or confused. DKA needs medical care right away
chapters.staying-safe.categories.7.note: The ladder below is from Breakthrough T1D and was written for type 1 diabetes. If you have another type, ask your team which numbers to use.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.7.title: Ketones: check and act
chapters.staying-safe.categories.8.figur: How often to check my blood sugar when I’m sick
When to check ketones, and blood or urine
My medicines to pause, and when to restart them (filled in with my pharmacist)
Foods and drinks I can manage when I’m sick
chapters.staying-safe.categories.8.note: Fill in the plan on this card with your pharmacist and diabetes team before you’re sick, so it’s ready when you need it.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.8.secti: Diabetes Canada’s sick-day sheet is for vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or a lot of heat or humidity without enough to drink: anything that can leave you dehydrated
What the sheet says to do
Drink plenty of fluids with little sugar, unless you’ve been told to limit fluids
If you can’t eat, the sheet lists foods with 15 g of carbohydrate to have instead
If you use insulin, check your blood sugar more often. The sheet says your insulin may need adjusting, so ask your team how
The sheet lists some medicines to stop for a short time if you’re eating less, or dehydrated, for more than 24 hours
Which of your own medicines this means is a question for your pharmacist. The sheet has a space for them to write it down
The sheet says to restart them once you’re eating and drinking normally
Vomiting and can’t keep fluids down: go to the emergency department. If you can reach your team right away, call them too

Call your team or go to the emergency department if you can’t drink enough, don’t know which medicines to stop or how to adjust your insulin, or your ketones are moderate. Large ketones need emergency care now
Do the same if vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, passing a lot of urine, extreme thirst, weakness or fever isn’t getting better. Trouble breathing needs emergency care now
chapters.staying-safe.categories.8.title: Sick days
chapters.staying-safe.categories.9.items: Diabetes Canada suggests keeping backup supplies, such as rapid-acting insulin pens or syringes, and learning how to switch to injections in case you can’t use your pump
If your blood sugar is high and you can’t explain it, check your ketones and follow the ladder in Ketones: check and act
Keep a written copy of your pump settings in your emergency kit
chapters.staying-safe.categories.9.note: Your pump team’s plan comes first. Ask them what to do if you think your pump has stopped giving insulin.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.9.title: On a pump: an unexplained high
chapters.staying-safe.categoriesIntro.bo: This chapter helps you follow the plan your diabetes team made with you, and shows when it’s time to call. If your team gave you different numbers, use theirs.
chapters.staying-safe.closing.body: Staying safe is the same few steps, practised: check, act, check again, and know when to call.

chapters.staying-safe.programsBand.cards: A low: take 15 g of fast-acting sugar, wait 15 minutes and check again. Still below 3.9? Take 15 g more. For a child, the amount depends on their age: see The Rule of 15.
Blood ketones 0.6 to 1.5 when you’re sick, or small urine ketones.
Blood ketones 1.5 to 3.0, or moderate urine ketones.
Can’t swallow, unconscious or having a seizure: call 911. Blood ketones over 3.0, large urine ketones, vomiting with no fluids kept down, or signs of DKA: get emergency care now.

chapters.staying-safe.urgent.action: Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.
chapters.staying-safe.urgent.heading: Get emergency care now
chapters.staying-safe.urgent.intro: Everyday lows and highs follow your plan. These don’t. Get emergency care now if the person:
chapters.staying-safe.urgent.signs.1: Can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure. Call 911, give glucagon if you have it, turn them on their side and stay with them. Don’t put food or drink in their mouth
chapters.staying-safe.urgent.signs.2: Is vomiting and can’t keep fluids down
chapters.staying-safe.urgent.signs.3: Has blood ketones above 3.0 mmol/L, or large ketones in their urine (ranges written for type 1 diabetes)
